units.unit: The student wants sources on how rent caps affect housing supply.
The student wants sources on what tenants actually want.
The student's current focus is supply: whether capping rents makes landlords pull flats off the market or stop building.
A source would need to compare places with hard rent caps against places without them or against lighter caps.
The source should show what happened to the number of units available.
Ideally the source would separate effects on sitting tenants from effects on people looking for a new place.
All five sources bear on supply and tenant preferences.
The student wants to check whether the working paper says hard caps on rent levels shrink supply while caps on increases within a tenancy barely do.
The student wants the paper's estimate of what a binding cut does to stock and to who gets pushed out.
The student wants the actual Hong Kong stock numbers to see whether supply moved while the ordinance was in force.
The student wants to read the passage on the cap distinction.
The student wants to read the passage on the binding cut and who gets pushed out.
The student wants to read the passage on the Hong Kong stock numbers.
The student needs cap-type evidence, binding-cut estimates, and Hong Kong stock numbers.
The student now needs the enforcement side: how much stock inspections actually cover.
The student wants to know whether a tenancy register would be feasible.
The student wants to know whether enforcement would reach the worst-off tenants or miss them.
The student wants the tenant voices: the man on the waiting list and the woman without a written agreement.
The coverage gap comes first: how little of the stock inspections actually reach.
The student wants to know whether a register could even be stood up.
Then who enforcement ends up missing.
The student wants the two tenant voices: the man on the waiting list and the woman with no written agreement.
The student wants figures on inspection coverage — what share of the stock gets inspected in a year.
The student wants to know how many staff it would take to run a tenancy register.
Then who enforcement ends up missing.
The student wants the two tenant voices: the man on the waiting list and the woman with no written agreement.
The student needs enforcement capacity, register staffing, and the two tenant voices.
The student still needs the legal side: whether a hard cap on initial rents could be challenged as taking away landlords' income.
The student wants to know how long such litigation would run.
The student wants to know whether a lighter indexed band would be defensible instead.
The student wants the landlords' own submission and how solid their cost figures are.
The source would support the claim that a hard cap on the first rent could be challenged in court as taking away landlords' income and that a case could run for years.
It would need to show the legal basis for such a challenge.
It would need to show roughly how long litigation would take.
It would need to show that a lighter indexed band on rents would be defensible as rate-capping rather than confiscation.
The landlords' submission is separate: the student wants to see whether their compliance-cost numbers are solid or just self-reported.
The student needs landlord cost figures and legal challenge evidence.
The working paper distinguishes first-generation hard caps on rent levels from second-generation caps on increases within tenancies.
First-generation controls show supply contraction; second-generation show small or null effects.
Berlin's rent freeze caused listings to shrink within a year as owners withheld flats.
When Berlin's law was struck down, suppressed increases released and new-contract rents jumped above the pre-cap trend.
New York's scheme stays light on first rents, which is why its stock contraction is modest.
Tightening first rents would push Hong Kong toward the Berlin situation.
Hong Kong should not impose a hard cap on initial SDU rents.
A narrower package of tenure security, an indexed rent band, enforcement investment, and a shorter public-housing queue is the better route.
The Berlin point came from D7's passages on listings shrinking within a year and rents jumping above trend after the cap fell.
The student wants independent backing for the same supply-contraction claim, ideally from the working paper's own modelling rather than just the Berlin case.
An estimate of how much stock a binding cap actually removes would strengthen the claim.
The student wants the working paper's own modelling estimate of how much stock a binding cap removes.
The student wants the working paper's own modelling of stock removed by a binding cap.
The student has already read D6's passages on the control-type distinction, the 10 percent removal estimate, and the 15 percent simulation.
The student wants to check the Berlin figures against the source itself before leaning on them.
The Berlin figures are evidence for the claim that a hard cap shrinks the supply of flats newcomers can find.
The Berlin figures are evidence that lifting the cap releases suppressed rents.
The student wants to read the Berlin passage on what happened to listings once the freeze was in force.
The student wants the Berlin note itself to confirm listing contraction and the post-cap rent jump.
The student has already read the Berlin passages on listings shrinking, rents jumping above trend, and caps binding differently on entrants than incumbents.
The student wants to nail down why a narrower package (tenure security, light indexed band, enforcement investment, shorter queue) beats a straight hard cap.
The student wants the source that argues for that package directly.
The source should supply evidence that the package actually works.
The source should show tenants would take tenure security and a faster queue over a nominal rent freeze, with survey numbers on what households would trade for what.
The student now has the Berlin and New York comparisons and the enforcement minute.
The student wants the tenants' own view: what they would trade for what and what they say would help most.
The student wants a survey or interview source on tenant views.
The NGO survey of 440 households and the interviews with Mr Chan and Mrs Wong are the sources for the tenants' own view.
The tenants' view supports two claims: tenants would give up a nominal rent freeze for tenure security or a faster flat offer, and their stated priority is the waiting list rather than rent.
The student wants the survey trade-off numbers and what Mr Chan says would help most.
The student has the trade-off numbers and Mr Chan's priority already.
The student still needs a source arguing directly for the narrow package over a hard cap.
Survey trade-offs, enforcement capacity, and tenant priorities all underpin the recommendation.
The NGO survey shows tenants would trade a nominal rent increase for tenure security and a faster flat offer.
The enforcement minute shows the register and inspection problem.
The student still needs to state the core reason: elasticity evidence cuts against a hard cap while a light band is safer.
A hard cap on the first rent acts on the margin where new tenants enter, shrinking supply of new subdivided flats and pushing the newest households out.
A light cap on increases inside a tenancy barely touches supply.
D6p2 carries the core reason: first-generation hard caps show consistent supply contraction while second-generation caps show small or null effects.
D6p2 already does the job for the core reason, so nothing more is needed there.
The student never put the headline recommendation (no hard cap, narrow package instead) into their own words.
The student never put the Berlin and New York comparisons into their own words.
The recommendation needs a source weighing a hard cap against a lighter package; the elasticity paper and enforcement minute together push toward the narrower package.
Berlin needs a source on what happened to listings under the Mietendeckel and what happened when it was struck down.
New York needs a source on how a light first-rent scheme behaves compared with a tight one.
The Berlin source should cover both the drop in listings under the Mietendeckel and the rebound in new-contract rents after it was struck down.
The Berlin evidence supports the claim that a hard cap binds differently on entrants than incumbents, so the bill lands on people still outside the segment.
